source: Consumers are often told a warranty is void because they used a third-party part; US law limits that, though it's not automatic in every situation.
card: Lorena, 45, in Arizona, USA, whose appliance maker denied a repair claim saying she voided the warranty by using a generic filter, and who now assumes she's out of luck. Frustrated but resigned, she writes in weary messages.
why_it_matters: The repair is expensive and she's ready to just pay it, believing she forfeited her warranty rights.
facts: The user has a product under manufacturer warranty
The manufacturer says that voided the warranty and denied a repair claim
The repair is expensive and she is inclined to just pay it
not_yet: You have not looked up the law on warranties and third-party parts
You have not yet paid for the repair or given up the warranty claim
You do not know whether the manufacturer's 'void' claim is actually lawful in your situation
anchor: Being told a warranty is 'void because you used a third-party part' doesn't mean it is - US law (the Magnuson-Moss Warranty Act) generally bars a manufacturer from voiding a warranty just because you used a generic part or independent service, unless they provide the part free or hold an FTC waiver. The nuance is that they can still deny a claim for damage the third-party part actually caused. So don't assume you've lost your rights without checking the law against your situation.
anchor_source: US FTC guidance on the Magnuson-Moss Warranty Act (15 U.S.C. 2302(c)): 'tie-in sales' provisions that condition warranty coverage on using branded parts/service are generally prohibited; a warranty isn't voided merely by using third-party parts, though coverage can be denied for damage those parts caused.
false_position: The manufacturer says my generic filter voided the whole warranty, so I've lost all my warranty rights and just have to pay for the repair myself.
evidence: The warranty text plus the Magnuson-Moss anti-tie-in rule show the maker generally can't void the warranty just for a generic part - and the fault here isn't one the filter caused.
evidence_source: Magnuson-Moss Warranty Act (FTC): a warrantor generally cannot void coverage because a consumer used a third-party part, unless it supplied the part free or holds an FTC waiver; blanket 'you used a generic part, so it's void' denials are improper where the part didn't cause the failure.
updated_position: Under Magnuson-Moss, the manufacturer generally can't void the whole warranty just because she used a generic filter (and the failure wasn't caused by that filter), so the blanket denial is improper and she can push back rather than simply pay.
